articles.summary: Candidato do PSD participou de entrevista em rádio e caminhada em Pedreiras; propostas incluem industrialização da produção e apoio técnico aos produtores rurais.
articles.body:
Os candidatos ao governo do Maranhão cumpriram agendas de campanha nesta segunda-feira (24) e apresentaram propostas voltadas para a agricultura, agricultura familiar e o agronegócio.

Felipe Camarão (PT), Eduardo Braide (PSD), Saulo Arcangeli (PSTU) e Roberto Rocha (PRTB) participaram de reuniões, entrevistas e encontros com apoiadores em diferentes regiões do estado.

A TV Mirante acompanhou os compromissos de campanha dos candidatos deste grupo e registrou as propostas apresentadas por cada um ao longo do dia.

Saiba como foi a agenda do candidato Eduardo Braide:

Eduardo Braide (PSD) — Foto: Reprodução/ TV Mirante

Eduardo Braide cumpriu agenda pela manhã em Pedreiras, na região do Médio Mearim. O candidato participou de uma entrevista em uma rádio local e depois realizou uma caminhada pela principal área comercial da cidade ao lado de aliados e apoiadores.

Entre as propostas apresentadas para o setor agrícola, Braide afirmou que pretende estimular a industrialização da produção maranhense e ampliar o apoio técnico aos produtores rurais.

Segundo o candidato, o objetivo é fazer com que produtos produzidos no Maranhão sejam industrializados no próprio estado, gerando emprego e renda para a população.

“Temos que atrair indústrias para que os produtos produzidos no Maranhão sejam industrializados. Assim, vamos fazer com que o emprego fique aqui no Maranhão”, declarou.

articles.title: Dan Sullivan endorses Dan Sullivan to beat Dan Sullivan in perplexing Alaska Senate race
articles.summary: A third Dan Sullivan — a former Anchorage mayor — has weighed in on the competitive Senate race, endorsing Sen. Dan S. Sullivan over former teacher Dan J. Sullivan.
articles.body: A new Dan Sullivan has entered the conversation surrounding the Alaska Senate race, in which incumbent Dan S. Sullivan faces a candidate with the same name. The Republican former mayor of Anchorage, Dan A. Sullivan, endorsed GOP Sen. Dan S. Sullivan for re-election over retired teacher Dan J. Sullivan and Democratic former Rep. Mary Peltola on Tuesday. “As the OG Dan Sullivan, I urge Alaskans to vote for Sen. Dan S. Sullivan. He’s been great for Alaska,” the former mayor wrote on Facebook. Both Dan S. Sullivan and Peltola advanced to the general election in November after the all-party primary last week, in which the top four finishers advance, regardless of political affiliation. NBC News has not yet made a call regarding who the other two candidates will be, but Dan J. Sullivan could be among them. Alaska’s Senate race is considered one of the most competitive this cycle, when control of the upper chamber hangs in the balance. With primary votes left to count, Peltola so far has 48% of the vote, with Sen. Dan S. Sullivan taking 43%. Dan J. Sullivan — who is running as a Republican — has 2.4%, with other candidates getting considerably fewer votes. The general election for the Senate race will be decided by ranked-choice voting. Democrats view the election as a seat they could flip in November. The Cook Political Report rates the race a toss-up. The Sullivan saga has drawn attention as former teacher Dan J. Sullivan’s candidacy has faced legal challenges. Dan S. Sullivan and Republicans have alleged that the teacher was placed on the ballot to confuse voters and detract from the senator’s share of the vote, claiming he’s working with Peltola. Dan J. Sullivan has denied coordinating with the Peltola campaign. Peltola has also denied any involvement with the second Sullivan campaign. The Alaska Supreme Court ruled last month that Dan J. Sullivan can stay on the ballot after the state Division of Elections originally disqualified him. NBC News has reported that state and federal prosecutors in Alaska were investigating whether the race could be part of a conspiracy to confuse voters. A grand jury issued subpoenas this month to compel information from witnesses linked to Dan J. Sullivan’s campaign. CORRECTION (Aug. 24, 2026, 4:14 p.m. ET): A previous version of this article mischaracterized the voting format for Alaska’s Senate primary. The state uses ranked-choice voting in the general election, not the primary.

articles.title: This democratic socialist has upset the party establishment. Here’s her strategy for Congress
articles.summary: As the Democratic Party’s socialist summer comes to a close, Darializa Avila Chevalier has become one of the most polarizing — and potentially most influenti...
articles.body:
This August's Dominican Heritage Reception at Gracie Mansion brought in a different crowd from years past.

Dozens of Dominican Americans, including activists more used to protesting than attending the event, mingled over trays of cheese empanadas and sancocho. Dressed in a butter yellow guayabera, New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani took a moment to shout out the notable community members in the crowd. The longest, loudest applause went to Darializa Avila Chevalier, the 32-year-old democratic socialist who defeated the chair of the Congressional Hispanic Caucus in June's Democratic primary.

Such friendly audiences, she knows, may become a rarity as she braces for Congress.

As the Democratic Party's socialist summer comes to a close, Avila Chevalier has become one of the most polarizing — and potentially most influential — faces of an insurgency that has bested several congressional incumbents and left the party at a crossroads.

Ahead of the midterms, the party is now grappling with the power Avila Chevalier and at least four other democratic socialist nominees could have if Democrats take back the House in November. If House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries wins a single-digit majority, the incoming cohort and its allies on the left could have huge sway over his potential speakership and demand concessions on a host of progressive priorities.

Already, Avila Chevalier and her allies are discussing how they want to lead and how they plan to work together.

"Our movement has worked too hard for me to allow myself to be distracted," Avila Chevalier told CNN. "We've been talking about how do we come in strong on day one, and really, meaningfully build a model of co-governance that gives power back to working people."

Avila Chevalier, a community organizer and doctoral student who centered her campaign on uncompromising support for Palestinians and abolishing Immigration and Customs Enforcement, has grown used to the noise surrounding her.

In the final weeks of her primary against Rep. Adriano Espaillat, much was made of her old tweets from a now-deleted account criticizing Democratic leaders and embracing far-left policies, as well as her attendance at a controversial rally in support of Palestinians the day after Hamas' October 7, 2023, attack on Israel. Avila Chevalier has since become a fixture on Fox News, a target of President Donald Trump's rallies, and a source of anxiety for House Democrats worried about being painted as socialists or communists by the GOP.

Progressives have urged party leadership to not fall into what they say is a familiar trap.

"Republicans are always encouraging us to divide ourselves," said Rep. Summer Lee, a progressive Pennsylvania Democrat. "I also see a lot of people who are trying to make her a boogeyman, who are trying to make her a pariah, and I am trying, and I really want to fight back against that instinct."

Similar dynamics played out after the 2018 midterms, when members of what became the "Squad" defeated longtime incumbents and quickly joined protests on Capitol Hill.

Some of those members, such as New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez — who did not endorse Avila Chevalier — have shown an ability to work within the caucus and across the aisle on key issues. Others, such as former Reps. Cori Bush of Missouri and Jamaal Bowman of New York, became better known for what they did outside the legislative process, leaving them vulnerable to successful primary challenges.

"It's one thing to be noisy, it's another thing to be intentional, and meaningful, and being able to deliver on the things you promise," said Antjuan Seawright, a Democratic strategist and longtime advisor to South Carolina Rep. Jim Clyburn.

Avila Chevalier is making the case that she's an organizer who is focused on making her platform a reality. Her challenge now is reintroducing herself to the party establishment she just took on.

"I am very concerned with delivering," she said. "I think folks will be, hopefully, pleasantly surprised about the fact that yes, I am really willing to talk to anybody, literally anybody, who wants to actually deliver for working people."

Avila Chevalier grew up in Florida, with brief stints in New York and Venezuela. Though her maternal grandfather was part of the resistance against dictator Rafael Trujillo back in the Dominican Republic, her family talked about politics in terms of the cost of gas or cuts to benefits. She, however, showed an interest in social justice early on.

Mariangelly Abreu, a distant relative she calls a cousin and who grew up alongside her, said Avila Chevalier would encourage them to buy flowers from the sellers on street corners instead of the supermarket and make other intentional choices about where they spent their money.

"My cousin can be — and I say this with so much love — annoyingly persistent," Abreu said. "She's not someone who will just say, 'Oh, well, that's just how things are.'"

Avila Chevalier applied to Columbia University to find a way to New York. Part of the school's appeal was that it was the "activist Ivy" and she soon joined the Black Student Organization and started organizing to end sexual assault on campus.

In her sophomore year, she came across a posting for a summer internship to teach English to Palestinians living in refugee camps in the West Bank. Her experience there, and the conditions she witnessed, helped shape the organizing work that would define her adult life and inspired her to convert to Islam.

"It was an opportunity for me to really get clear on what my values are, on what it means to advocate for human dignity even when it's politically hard, even when there is so much that is pushing you to stay silent on things," she said.

Some of the highs and lows of her campaign trace back to that trip and the work in which she subsequently engaged. Avila Chevalier became an active member of Students for Justice in Palestine, and returned to Columbia as an alumna to support students as they took over part of the campus in 2024 to protest Israel's military actions in Gaza. There she worked alongside Mahmoud Khalil, a fellow organizer who was later detained by the Trump administration for more than three months.

Avila Chevalier pointed to her West Bank experience to justify her presence at the October 8th rally, held in support of Gaza the day after Hamas attacked Israel, that featured speech and rhetoric praising the attack, in which 1,200 Israelis were killed and 250 more kidnapped. According to reports, pro-Palestinian protesters chanted "from the river to the sea, Palestine will be free" and "resistance is justified, when people are colonized."

Soon after she returned to the US in 2014, Hamas militants kidnapped and killed three Israeli teenagers, triggering a military response from Israel that killed an estimated 2,251 Palestinians. Avila Chevalier said she feared a similar large-scale counter-response in 2023. An estimated 70,000 people have died in Gaza in the war after October 7th.

Asked if there's anything she feels she needs to apologize for regarding the rally, Avila Chevalier said, "There are people who've expressed views in spaces like this who you don't always agree with." But she said she hoped those who attended pro-Israel rallies where some attendees have made inflammatory remarks would also reject those comments.

Avila Chevalier's organizing and academic work on immigration has fueled her belief that ICE must be abolished and that all deportations are wrong. Before running for Congress, she worked with Families for Freedom to try to block deportations and spent three years attending deportation hearings and interviewing people caught up in the process as part of her PhD in sociology at the City University of New York.

Late last year, Avila Chevalier called her adviser, Professor David Brotherton, to say she was being recruited to challenge Espaillat and would be unlikely to complete her dissertation on time if she decided to run.

"I said, 'No, I don't think you probably are,'" he recalled telling her. "If it's a question of making history or writing a dissertation, I would choose the former."

Early last year, Avila Chevalier reached out to Justice Democrats, the same progressive group that recruited Ocasio-Cortez, to see if there was a window for someone to primary Espaillat.

Over his five terms in Congress — and several decades as a state legislator and local political leader — Espaillat had built up a formidable political presence in the district, including local officials he'd mentored known as the "Squadriano." Avila Chevalier and other Espaillat critics argued the congressman was absent from the district.

A spokesperson for Espaillat pushed back on that assessment, noting his work on immigration cases, pandemic recovery and affordable housing. "Soon, campaigning and slogans have to give way to governing and leading," the spokesperson said in a statement.

Those early talks of a challenge lapsed until Mamdani, a democratic socialist, won the district in last year's mayoral primary.

Last August, Geoff Simpson, Justice Democrats' PAC director emailed her about running after local organizers recommended her. It took two and a half months of conversations to convince her to run, he said.

"People like to get plugged in at the end with like the TV ads and the messaging," Simpson said. "But if you get the candidate recruitment piece wrong, none of that ends up mattering."

Ahead of her launch, the group targeted two key and ambitious endorsements: the New York City Democratic Socialists of America, which was wading into congressional races for the first time, and Mamdani, who had been endorsed by Espaillat in the mayoral general election.

During an endorsement meeting earlier this year, NYC-DSA co-chair Gustavo Gordillo worried the group wouldn't be able to both challenge Espaillat and back Assemblymember Claire Valdez in the open 7th Congressional District.

"I wasn't sure if we would be able to meet the moment, and I'm really glad that members proved me wrong, and we did," he told CNN.

His support drew attention to the race, as well as her record.

News outlets, including CNN , reported on tweets Avila Chevalier either personally wrote or reposted between 2018 and 2022 on a since-deleted account. Some — including a post that called on people to "become bad bitches" and "seize the means of production" — were written in the flippant, ironic tone favored by far-left online posters. But several made serious calls for defunding and abolishing the police and criticized Israel and Democratic politicians. After former Vice President Kamala Harris made a speech telling Central American migrants "do not come" to the United States, Avila Chevalier tweeted, "F**k Kamala Harris."

Avila Chevalier said she's grown since using that language and regrets her post history. In reflecting on the account, she said she was part of a generation that came of age online.

"We are the first generation to really be forming our sense of self and our political identities and our political worldviews in such a public way, and that inevitably means that we're going to say things that we'll eventually not agree with or feel cringe about or regret," she said.

Avila Chevalier said it was painful to see her deleted tweets become a distraction from the issues she wanted to highlight. At the same time, she said it wasn't lost on her that the words of a 20-something with no political power were being dissected while "we have folks who have been in political power for almost as long as I've been alive, or longer, who have passed policy that have cost people their lives."

"That is at the heart of the problem that we've had for so long, is that accountability feels unreachable in our political system," she said.

It's not clear how the House Democratic Caucus will respond to Avila Chevalier or the other Justice Democrats and DSA-aligned candidates who won blue district primaries this cycle, but early indicators suggest a mix of wariness, defiance and, in some cases, cautious optimism.

Publicly, party leadership has congratulated them. But moderate Democrats are also making a point of spurning socialism to reduce the sting of Republican attacks.

Jeffries said earlier this month on NBC's Meet the Press that he rejects the national Democratic Socialists of America agenda, wants to reform but not abolish ICE and no longer supports Medicare for All after previously co-sponsoring the bill. But he acknowledged the party will have a "broad caucus" in January.

The challenge for Avila Chevalier is that, as of now, there is a perception that she is more of an activist than a coalition builder.

The difference is activism is about calling attention to an issue, said Ilona Duverge, Avila Chevalier's campaign manager. "An organizer," she said, "is going to think of 'What are the steps, what is the path that I need to forge in order to actually meet my goal?'"

Avila Chevalier has three top priorities, what she described on the campaign trail as housing for all, "babies not bombs," and abolishing ICE. Among the 13 bills she's promised to cosponsor on her first day of Congress is Illinois Rep. Delia Ramirez's Block the Bombs Act, which would stop the unconditional transfer of offensive military weapons to Israel. She'll also back the Green New Deal, Medicare for All Act, and legislation to boost unions and raise the federal minimum wage.

Ramirez said she's been vocal with leadership about making sure Avila Chevalier as well as the other far-left primary winners feel welcome in DC. She described the New York candidate as someone who asks questions, "genuinely wants to grow, wants to learn" and wants to fight for the district.

"She also understands she can't come here and spend 20 years here before she can deliver," Ramirez said.

The likely incoming members are also still figuring out how they'll wield their influence in what could be a very narrow House Democratic majority.

"The most important thing is that we're getting into the habit of calling each other when we have questions," said Valdez, the Democratic nominee for the 7th District who is also backed by Mamdani, the DSA and Justice Democrats. "We're still figuring out what the demands will be."

In the meantime, the nominees have been focused on building up their support in their districts. For Avila Chevalier, that's meant meet-and-greets and community events.

Earlier this month she joined New York state Sen. Gustavo Rivera to hand out backpacks and school supplies to a long line of families that wrapped around a park in the South Bronx, a part of the district that heavily favored the incumbent. Rivera, who didn't endorse in the primary but said he voted for Avila Chevalier, introduced the Democratic nominee to constituents as they went through the line, often in Spanish.

"There's many people, many voters as well as electeds in this part of the district, that had a longstanding relationship with Congressmember Espaillat," Rivera told CNN in an interview at the event. "That ship has sailed. She actually won the seat. Now it's her job to actually do this type of work."

Sometimes that has forced her to confront voters whose views are far from her own. During her interview with CNN, Avila Chevalier was flagged down by a group of voters sitting in Marcus Garvey Park. The Democratic nominee struck up a conversation with Monique Wyche, a restaurant employee and small business owner who grew up in Harlem.

When Wyche brought up the Iran War, Avila Chevalier argued that the money spent on it could have gone towards universal childcare. When the topic turned to immigration, Wyche said that while ICE's actions were "sick," she was concerned about migrants not paying taxes, a claim Avila Chevalier quickly refuted.

"Actually, they do get taxed," Avila Chevalier said. "I think that narrative actually benefits corporations, and so they don't pay taxes."

The two went back and forth for nearly 10 minutes, with Wyche calling on Avila Chevalier to work with both Republicans and Democrats while also charting her own path in Congress.

That is what Avila Chevalier says she signed up for — having hard conversations with people to make sense of the world and bridge the gap between what exists and what could be – and what she hopes to bring to Congress next year.

"Organizing is about meeting people where they're at," she said. "It is deeply unsexy work."

articles.title: ‘Radical’ has become the political word of the summer
articles.summary: As campaigns prepare for the crucial fall stretch ahead of the midterm elections, the word “radical” is being slung against candidates on both sides of the aisle. It’s happening as both parties are pulled from the political center, and it’s being used by Republicans against Democrats and Democrats against Republicans to make the same argument:…
articles.body:
As campaigns prepare for the crucial fall stretch ahead of the midterm elections, the word “radical” is being slung against candidates on both sides of the aisle.

It’s happening as both parties are pulled from the political center, and it’s being used by Republicans against Democrats and Democrats against Republicans to make the same argument: My opponent has moved outside the mainstream.

Republicans, often on their heels because of negative headwinds from the economy and the war in Iran, have used the term regularly as a weapon against “radical” Democrats.

From President Trump down to congressional campaigns, the GOP is eager to shift attention to how the rise of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) and the left rank of the Democratic Party in general is “radical” or “extreme.”

Democrats, for their part, have used “radical” as a way to describe Trump and his MAGA movement, arguing it is time to put a curb on the GOP.

“Radical is the current word of choice in the framing battle to set the agenda for the 2026 elections,” said Tobe Berkovitz, a communications professor emeritus at Boston University who has served as a political consultant. “The Democrats and Republicans both use it to position their opponents as far out of touch with current social and political norms.

“For framing to succeed, words must be used repeatedly to sink into the minds of the voter,” Berkovitz added. “‘Radical’ certainly fits that criteria.”

For both Republicans and Democrats, “the partisan struggle to define ‘radical will be a very important part of the campaign cycle,” said Julian Zelizer, a professor of history and public affairs at Princeton University.

The race to define the meaning of the word has been at the forefront of political battles around the country.

In Florida, GOP Rep. Byron Donalds, who is campaigning for governor, has been using the word in a political ad against his opponent, Democrat David Jolly, who used to be a Republican House member.

“How radical is David Jolly on the trans agenda?” the 30-second spot begins.

It continues by saying that Jolly is “radically liberal, radically wrong.”

“The only way you defeat crazy is stand up to it,” Donalds says in the conclusion of the ad.

The use of radical extended to the back-and-forth between the White House and Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-Ga.), who is up for reelection in November, after Ossoff slammed Trump for not prioritizing his job as president.

“He golfs and trades stocks. … He wants to build a ballroom and travel with Natalie on their apparently defenseless flying palace gifted by the emir of Qatar,” Ossoff said at a rally last weekend, referencing White House aide Natalie Harp and beginning a days-long feud with the White House.

White House Communications Director Steven Cheung responded by slamming Ossoff for being “a radical, extremist” Democrat.

Trump has time and again referred to Democrats as “radical” or “the radical left,” but he refrained from using the rhetoric when he was asked about Ossoff by a reporter in the Oval Office. The president simply called him “Pee-wee Herman” after the comic personality played by the late actor Paul Reubens.

Democrats — from individual campaigns to EMILY’s List, the Democratic PAC that helps elect women — have also made radical part of their regular vernacular.

Earlier this month, for example, the Democratic Governors Association released an ad highlighting Rep. Tom Tiffany’s (R-Wis.) “radical agenda.” Tiffany is facing off against David Crowley in the closely watched Wisconsin gubernatorial race.

“Pandering politician Tom Tiffany pretends he’s anything but a congressman with a MAGA agenda,” a narrator says. “The truth? Tiffany’s agenda is so radical that even Republicans say he’s part of a group of legislative terrorists in Congress.”

In Illinois, Gov. JB Pritzker, up for reelection, has been knocking his opponent Darren Bailey for being too radical. In a new ad called “Too Extreme,” Pritzker targets his opponent’s views opposing abortion, including in cases of rape and incest, as well as his loyalty to Trump and his “radical” pro-gun rhetoric.

Political observers say the word perfectly describes the polarization of the moment.

“It means more now than it ever did before,” said Susan Del Percio, the veteran Republican strategist. “It’s actually more reflective of where both parties are now.”

“It’s an exclamation point on the ideas, and it’s shorthand for out of the norm,” Del Percio added.

But Del Percio, who does not support Trump, said using the word in a broad-sweeping way is “ineffective.”

“It’s laughable in some cases because someone like David Jolly is anything but radical,” she said. “He’s a former Republican and is much more independent minded. You can’t take the DSA movement and their ideas and impose that on David Jolly.”

She suggested it’s much more effective for Republican Mike Rogers to use the label on someone like Abdul El-Sayed in the Michigan Senate race. “His policies are associated with radical ideas,” she said.

But Republican strategist Brian Seitchik said the word resonates with voters because “it transforms Democratic policy disagreements into a warning about the people proposing it.”

“It makes Democrats not just wrong but willing to remake the world with their policies that are not mainstream, that do not resonate with the American people,” Seitchik said. “We are not a socialist country. We are not Europe, despite the socialist agenda that is taking over the Democratic Party.”

Still, Seitchik cautioned, “You can’t just point and say ‘radical.’ You have to have some meat on the bones. And thankfully Democrats are giving us plenty of opportunities to do that.”

Michael Eric Dyson, the renowned historian and author, called the rhetoric the Red Scare 2.0, particularly for Republicans — and even for some moderate Democrats — who have seen the rise of candidates like Zohran Mamdani in New York, El-Sayed in Michigan, and Angie Nixon in Florida.

As the races heat up, he and others predicted, the rhetoric will only ramp up.

“It’s definitely a scare tactic,” Dyson said. “When you ain’t got much to say you got to do that. You got to play the card you got. And it’s a joker.”

articles.title: Iowa Senate candidates zero in on cancer crisis as key race tightens
articles.summary: Candidates for Iowa’s open Senate seat are zeroing in on the state’s high rate of cancer diagnoses as the race emerges as one of the most unexpectedly competitive contests this cycle. The race features Democratic state legislator Josh Turek challenging Republican Rep. Ashley Hinson (Iowa) for the seat held by retiring Iowa Sen. Joni Ernst…
articles.body:
Candidates for Iowa’s open Senate seat are zeroing in on the state’s high rate of cancer diagnoses as the race emerges as one of the most unexpectedly competitive contests this cycle.

The race features Democratic state legislator Josh Turek challenging Republican Rep. Ashley Hinson (Iowa) for the seat held by retiring Iowa Sen. Joni Ernst (R). The Cook Political Report, a nonpartisan election analyst, last week moved the state’s Senate contest from “lean Republican” to “toss-up.”

Turek, a two-time Paralympic gold medalist in basketball, is emphasizing his bipartisan record, trying to pitch himself as an independent voice. His latest ad notes that he has voted with Republicans in the statehouse 700 times. Hinson, a former broadcast journalist, is leaning on her record leading bipartisan bills and overseeing appropriations in the House. She also carries an endorsement from President Trump.

But an X factor is each candidate’s approach to Iowa’s cancer rates, which are some of the worst in the country. Iowa has the second-highest incidence rate for cancer in the nation, behind only Kentucky, and that rate is rising while most of the country’s incidence rates are stable or decreasing.

Kerri Johannsen, the senior director of policy and programs at the Iowa Environmental Council (IEC), said knowing many people with cancer was common around the state when she and her team started researching the crisis last summer.

“We all knew a lot of people, of course, who had cancer,” Johannsen said. “But I think that there was an idea that it was kind of just normal.”

The biggest culprits, according to IEC’s research, are environmental contaminants, especially PFAS, nitrates, radon and pesticides — the levels of which are higher in Iowa than other states.

“You can’t ever say like, ‘This thing caused this cancer,’ but we do have what we call kind of a skyscraper of risk factors,” Johannsen said. “And when you start to say, okay, well, maybe you have radon in your home. That’s a carcinogen. On top of that, perhaps you’ve had exposure to pesticides or nitrate in your drinking water. Each of those things, when they stack on top of each other, increases the risk of developing cancer.”

The prominence of pesticides and nitrates, in particular, are due to the heavily agricultural economy that makes Iowa run.

Johannsen said those spreading awareness of the issue have to carefully thread a needle between discussing solutions and not demonizing the agriculture industry that is the backbone of the state.

“I’m a farmer’s daughter,” Johannsen said, noting that while she understands “this is a tough thing to talk about,” the IEC has found that “the elephant in the room when it comes to this issue is: What part is our industrialized agricultural system playing in this crisis?”

“Many people in Iowa already were feeling and suspecting this was a part of the problem,” she continued.

The candidates for political offices are taking that balance seriously.

Turek has been talking a lot about cancer as he travels the state. He has told stories about his grandmother, who died of pancreatic cancer; his father, who was exposed to Agent Orange and had a variety of health complications including cancer; and his sister, who was diagnosed with Stage 2 breast cancer the day Turek launched his campaign for Senate.

His message is focused on cracking down on insurance companies so patients have more access to care they can afford.

“I talk a lot about healthcare as a human right, and that if I’m able to get to the U.S. Senate, I want to fight for a public option to make sure that every single American has access to a baseline level of healthcare coverage,” he said in an interview with Ability Magazine published earlier this month.

Hinson, in a statement to The Hill, said she supports efforts to address the growing cancer rate by expanding access to detection and care.

“I’m proud to co-lead legislation that would improve access to mammogram machines, mobile cancer screening tools, and other preventative equipment in rural areas,” Hinson said. “We’ve got way more to do – I’ll keep fighting for results that help families fight cancer and save lives.”

Hinson also introduced a bill recently that would redirect revenue from existing taxes on tobacco into cancer research, and a spokesperson pointed to her involvement in passing the Rural Health Transformation Fund as part of last year’s Republican reconciliation package, the One Big Beautiful Bill.

The focus on cancer rates comes as the race for Senate tightens.

A red stronghold for the past decade, the agricultural prairie state has taken a heavy hit from Trump’s tariffs and rising fertilizer prices. At the same time, Republican candidates nationwide are bogged down by the Trump administration’s low approval ratings.

In announcing the seat’s shift to “toss-up,” the Cook Political Report’s Jessica Taylor wrote that “the political environment is uniquely challenging for the GOP” in Iowa.

An Emerson College poll earlier this month found Hinson leading Turek, 48 percent to 45 percent, within the poll’s credibility interval. Six percent of respondents were undecided.

The Cook report also shifted the governor’s race from “toss-up” to “lean Democrat.” And the gubernatorial candidates, Democrat Rob Sand and Republican Zach Lahn, have made a central issue of addressing the cancer crisis.

Sand this week took it a step further, using headlines about a new mRNA treatment for melanoma to bash Lahn over his skepticism of mRNA vaccines.

Lahn, speaking at an American Cancer Society Cancer Action Network roundtable on Tuesday, singled out water quality as a cause for colon and ovarian cancer rates rising and said addressing contaminants in Iowa’s food and water supply is a “major, major focus.” He has also talked about his father’s battle with non-Hodgkin lymphoma.

Timothy Hagle, a professor of political science at the University of Iowa, said he’d seen the cancer crisis showing up in races all across the ballot, including the three competitive House races. In particular, Democrats are hitting Republicans over their votes to cut cancer research and funding for care in the reconciliation bill last year.

“I did see at least a couple of ads, not from Turek directly, but from some of the PACs that are advertising against Hinson, that kind of were chastising her for votes that she took in Congress, and so it’s sort of an indirect way to get at some of these medical issues,” Hagle said.

Turek has said as much on the campaign trail.

“Looking at a state with a legitimate healthcare crisis,” Turek said in June. “Only state with a growing cancer rate. Closed 250 more healthcare clinics than we’ve opened and what has she [Hinson] done? She has voted to see 110,000 Iowans lose their healthcare.”

But Hagle predicted the race will mostly turn on more conventional issues, like name recognition. Turek is still trying to introduce himself to voters, Hagle said, while Hinson as a U.S. representative is better-known. It’s the reverse in the governor’s race, though, where Sand as state auditor cut an outsized profile and is making pains to distinguish himself from other Democrats.

“The hope is that to the extent that Sand might actually win, that he’ll cause the other Democrats and the other competitive races to do better, which is probably one of the reasons why some people think that the Senate race is a toss-up at this point,” Hagle said. “But I’m just not buying it, at least not yet.”

articles.title: Four states where Democrats are running away from their own brand
articles.summary: A party confident in its own name doesn’t need to find ways not to use it.
articles.body:
When Democrat David Roth suspended his U.S. Senate campaign in Idaho on July 28, he did not mention the man his exit was intended to benefit. Todd Achilles, a former Democratic state representative, is now running as an independent against Sen. Jim Risch (R-Idaho). When he called it a two-person race, he didn’t mention Roth either.

Neither man wanted to draw attention to what had just happened.

That silence was notable, because this wasn’t an isolated incident. It’s the third time this cycle a Democratic Senate nominee has stepped aside to let a supposedly independent candidate — or at least someone without an official “D” next to his name — take the field alone against a Republican incumbent.

Individually, each case looks like a local story about a longshot candidate fizzling out. Together, though they look like a nationwide Democratic strategy — something the party would certainly never admit to, and one that says more about the state of the Democratic brand than its leaders likely want to discuss.

In Nebraska, Cindy Burbank won the Democratic Senate primary in May after openly promising she would drop out if she saw no path to victory. She kept that promise on July 17, exiting the race just as independent Dan Osborn qualified for the ballot by petition. This set up a one-on-one race against Sen. Pete Ricketts (R-Neb.). The secretary of state had already tried to remove Burbank from the ballot for not being a “good-faith candidate.” She sued her way back on, then dropped out to help Osborn, exactly as expected.

In South Dakota, Democrat Julian Beaudion dropped out in early August after months of insisting he’d never quit the race. A former state trooper, Beaudion looked like an ideal Democratic candidate on paper. But the challenge to Sen. Mike Rounds (R-N.D.) will now fall to independent Brian Bengs, a former Democrat who was trounced by Sen. John Thune (R-S.D.) in 2022.

In Idaho, the Ada County Democratic Central Committee — covering Boise, the state’s Democratic stronghold — sent Roth a public ultimatum in early July: Raise real money and produce a new plan, or the party would consider endorsing Achilles instead. Roth had raised just over $8,000 to Achilles’ $700,000 and Risch’s $3.5 million. Roth called the demand “ridiculous” and vowed to stay in, but three weeks later, he dropped out without explanation.

The same conversation is happening in Montana. Democratic nominee Alani Bankhead (D) has so far refused pressure to withdraw in favor of independent Seth Bodnar, even after the state party chair was found to have quietly solicited legal advice on handling a potential vacancy.

Four states, four Republican-held Senate seats, four Democratic parties pulling or considering the same maneuver of vacating their own ballot line so that a technically unaffiliated candidate can run without the baggage of the Democratic label.

None of this is illegal, and it’s not new — Angus King and Bernie Sanders have caucused with Senate Democrats for years without anyone calling it a scandal. What’s new is the intentionality. National Democrats aren’t just tolerating friendly independents anymore; in at least two of these races, state party infrastructure actively worked to clear the field for them.

It makes a certain amount of sense. In states like these, “Democrat” is usually a losing brand in statewide races, regardless of a candidate’s actual positions. An independent can absorb anti-incumbent energy and deep-red dissatisfaction with national Republicans in ways a Democratic nominee simply cannot, no matter how moderate that nominee might be.

Timing matters, too. These withdrawals are landing just as centrist Democrats panic over the rise of the Democratic Socialists of America. The New York Times recently reported that Third Way and other centrist organizations are preparing for what one leader called the “next war” — not against Republicans, but against the party’s own socialist wing, newly emboldened by Senate primary victories by Michigan’s Abdul El-Sayed (D) and Florida’s Angie Nixon (D).

Democrats are purging their brand from red-state ballots and bracing for a civil war over that same brand everywhere else. When a party isn’t sure what it stands for, it is easier just not to say anything.

Idaho Democrats had made a habit of swapping candidates on their own ballot line, but the legislature closed that loophole in 2025, declaring that the winner of the primary must be the candidate in November, barring death or disqualification. Simply withdrawing in favor of an independent does not violate that law, but it is still a betrayal of the party’s own voters.

How voters respond to this nationwide strategy remains to be seen. The independents in these four races still trail their Republican opponents in the polls and in fundraising. But the strategy tells on itself. A party confident in its own name doesn’t need to find ways not to use it. Is that shrewd coalition building? Or a quiet admission of brand failure? It depends on which Democrat you ask.

Brian Almon is chairman of Idaho’s District 14 Republican Party, a trustee of the Eagle Public Library Board, and editor of the Gem State Chronicle.

articles.title: Canadian anger reaches fever pitch over Trump’s tariff war
articles.summary: In today’s issue: ▪ Canada pledges tit-for-tat tariffs ▪ Jeffries, Kushner meet ahead of midterms ▪ Economic ‘D-Day’ for Iran ▪ House Ethics Committee under pressure Canada’s political leaders have united to rally the country against President Trump in a brewing trade war after Prime Minister Mark Carney walked away from talks on Friday just hours before new…
articles.body:
▪ Jeffries, Kushner meet ahead of midterms

Canada’s political leaders have united to rally the country against President Trump in a brewing trade war after Prime Minister Mark Carney walked away from talks on Friday just hours before new 50 percent tariffs took effect.

Carney told reporters at a press conference in Ottawa that his government will “match Washington’s new tariffs dollar for dollar.” Retaliatory tariffs are set to take effect on Sept. 8.

Carney said he broke off negotiations reluctantly because he knows the tariffs will result in higher costs for Canadians.

“But at the same time, we take this step confident that it is in the best interest of Canada,” he said.

“You’re at war when you’re attacked, and we got attacked,” Carney added. “We cannot accept what they’ve offered and we will not give what they’ve asked.”

Canadian politicians across the political spectrum have backed Carney’s move, including opposition leader Pierre Poilievre of the Conservative Party.

“Canadians must stand united to defend our country against these unfair attacks on our jobs and businesses,” he wrote on the social platform X after talks broke down. “Canada cannot accept one-sided tariffs that will deindustrialize our country. Nor can we accept a bad deal. Instead, we must continue the fight for tariff-free trade.”

Provincial premiers struck a similar note.

“I’m sure there is a desire to get back to the table, but we should recognize that the Trump administration and the president are deeply flawed. He’s got two more years left in office. We should be prepared to duke it out for two years. And then hopefully sanity will return to America,” Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew told reporters .

“It will be painful, but we have a strong, vibrant, diversified economy,” said Ontario Premier Doug Ford , who has led Canada’s opposition to Trump’s trade policies.

“We have to use every tool in our toolbox to make sure as Donald Trump is trying to inflict pain on every Canadian that we inflict pain right back,” he added in remarks to reporters.

Conservative Alberta Premier Danielle Smith expressed concern about the impact of a trade war but said the U.S.’s terms in negotiations were “untenable” for Canada to accept.

Trump is not enjoying similar unity behind his trade policies, which have been among the most controversial aspects of his second term.

Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine), a moderate who is in the midst of a tough reelection battle, urged the administration to “consider the negative impact” of engaging in a trade war with Canada. She said the tariffs would result in higher costs for Mainers.

“Ever since the tariffs were first announced, I have heard from many businesses, farmers, and lobstermen concerned about the cost of navigating the tariffs, the lack of domestic supply chains, and the likely imposition of retaliatory tariffs by Canada,” she said in a post on X . “I urge both sides to return to the negotiating table.”

Democrats were predictably furious over the development, with figures including Sen. Amy Klobuchar , who is running for governor of Minnesota, and New York Gov. Kathy Hochul warning that prices would go up for U.S. consumers.

The U.S. and Canada had seemed to be approaching a deal that would stave off the 50 percent tariffs from going into effect on more than $20 billion worth of Canadian goods through much of last week.

The tariffs affect a wide range of goods, including wine, cement, plywood, furniture and hockey sticks.

Carney said “significant progress” was made in recent weeks but accused the U.S. of seeking to change the terms at the last minute.

U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer argued in an interview with The New York Times that the U.S. proposal would have given Canada the most preferential treatment of any trading partner.

He said the Trump administration would have eliminated a 10 percent tariff on softwood lumber and reduce a 25 percent tariff on cars that were imposed last year. He said the U.S. also offered to lower tariffs on metals, including steel and aluminum.

Carney said at the press conference that Canada agreed to many U.S. demands, including lifting various retaliatory tariffs and convincing Canadian provinces to lift bans on the sale of U.S. liquor. But he said the U.S. refused to include exemptions for some Canadian trucks and subsidies for French culture.

Trump showed no signs of backing down Sunday, alleging Canada wants the “benefits of being a state, without being one.”

“They have also charged our great farmers, for many years, massive amounts of Tariffs. No more!!!” he said on Truth Social.

▪ The Hill : Sean Duffy says Carney will ‘come to the table.’

▪ Politico : Inside the 72 hours that cratered the U.S.-Canada deal.

California Attorney General Rob Bonta has called off settlement talks with Paramount over the state’s lawsuit against its planned acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery. Bonta, one of 12 state attorneys general suing the company, accused Paramount of leaking details of a meeting they held Friday and misrepresenting the talks.

U.S. Southern Command carried out an airstrike on an alleged drug trafficking boat in the East Pacific, the first known such strike in two months. Southcom said two people were killed in the attack. More than 200 people have been killed over the past year and a half of U.S. strikes in the Pacific and the Caribbean.

Sean Grayson, the former sheriff’s deputy convicted of fatally shooting Sonya Massey at her home in Illinois in 2024, has died in prison at age 32 after just six months into his 20-year sentence. He was previously denied early release as he was suffering from advanced colon cancer.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) speaks during a news conference on Capitol Hill, on July 13, 2026, in Washington. (AP Photo/Jose Luis Magana )

MEETING OF THE MINDS : House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries (N.Y.) and the president’s son-in-law Jared Kushner met in private in recent weeks to discuss possible areas of common ground, five people with knowledge of the meeting told The New York Times .

The meeting is being interpreted as a sign of the administration’s acknowledgement of the likelihood that Democrats win back control of the House in November.

The Decision Desk HQ forecast model currently gives Democrats roughly a 2 in 3 chance of winning a majority this fall.

Two people told the Times that Jeffries and Kushner discussed housing, immigration and the cost of living as potential areas of progress, and Kushner suggested Jeffries could meet with White House chief of staff Susie Wiles .

House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) downplayed the significance of the meeting during an appearance on Fox News’s “The Sunday Briefing,” noting that Kushner doesn’t have an official position within the administration. Kushner has served as an informal envoy for the president in talks to end the conflicts in Ukraine, Gaza and Iran.

Trump and Jeffries have often clashed since the president’s return to officer. However, Trump told Punchbowl News earlier this month that he believes Jeffries is a “nice guy” with whom he could do business.

The Times reported that Kushner has told Trump’s advisers that if any bipartisan accomplishments are to get done in Congress, Jeffries, a fellow New Yorker, is the most serious person among Democratic leaders.

▪ The Hill : ‘Shocking’ fake poll firm puts industry under the microscope.

▪ The Hill : ‘Radical’ has become the political word of the summer.

‘D-DAY’ ARRIVING : Senate Majority Whip John Barrasso (R-Wyo.) said Monday will be economic “D-Day” for Iran as Trump has vowed to inflict maximum economic pressure on the country to force it to agree to end the war.

“Their economy is in shambles. And they’re still dangerous. So, the president’s right to focus on it. And now he’s going even further economically. And as you said, tomorrow is D-Day for the economy in Iran,” Barrasso said on Fox News’s “Sunday Morning Futures.”

The Trump administration’s main tool for the economic offensive is the use of secondary sanctions, in which the U.S. will penalize foreign nations, banks and businesses that work with Iran economically.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent is scheduled to reveal the full details of the plan at a press conference today.

“We are now entering the endgame,” Bessent wrote on X, teasing an article he wrote for The Financial Times . “At dawn begins an economic D-Day — the single greatest financial offensive ever marshaled against an adversary.”

Iran has warned its neighbors in the region against joining the U.S. in an “economic war” against Tehran, saying it will “retaliate in a seismic manner” if Trump takes action.

▪ The Hill Insider : Trump’s ‘economic D-Day’ on Iran puts China in the crosshairs.

▪ The Hill : Mike Pence says more U.S. strikes against Iran ‘inevitable.’

▪ PBS : Iran’s president says U.S. memorandum is best way out of war.

RUNWAY CLEAR : The Trump administration has begun deportation flights of migrants previously protected under temporary protected status (TPS) after the last roadblock was lifted.

A federal judge lifted the final stay that barred immigration authorities from carrying out deportations to Ethiopia last week, the last of various court cases from TPS recipients challenging the elimination of their protections.

There are 13 countries formerly part of TPS that past administrations deemed not stable enough because of civil unrest or natural disasters to safely return migrants. Rebecca Beitsch reports for The Hill’s Insider that the designations for four other countries still part of TPS are set to expire soon, meaning more than 1.3 million migrants either have or will likely soon lose their protected status.

“Effectively, this signals the end of the program,” Nayna Gupta , policy director at the American Immigration Council, told Beitsch.

The moves come after the Supreme Court’s ruling in June that courts didn’t have the power to review the administration’s decision to end protections for citizens of Haiti and Syria.

▪ The Hill : Florida Republican ‘working’ with Haiti to stabilize government.

▪ The Hill : Federal judge rules against Trump’s 75-country visa ban.

The president will participate in a Rose Garden event at 2:30 p.m. He will participate in two telerallies at 6 p.m. and 7 p.m.

The House will convene at 9 a.m. for a pro forma session.

The Senate will meet at 12:30 p.m. for a pro forma session.

Rep. Max Miller (R-Ohio) arrives for new member orientation check-in and program registration in Washington, Nov. 13, 2022.

HURRY UP : Democrats and Republicans are calling on the House Ethics Committee to move more expeditiously in its investigations into members accused of sexual misconduct or domestic violence.

The probes into Reps. Cory Mills (R-Fla.), Max Miller (R-Ohio) and Jimmy Gomez (D-Calif.) have dominated headlines for weeks and left the public in limbo as the latter two are seeking reelection in November. Mills was defeated in his primary last week.

“One of the long-standing problems of House Ethics investigations is that they simply take too long — staff, the public, and the Members need the investigations and reporting to be quicker and responsive,” Rep. Teresa Leger Fern ández (D-N.M.), the chair of the Democratic Women’s Caucus, told The Hill’s Sudiksha Kochi .

Rep. Anna Paulina Luna (R-Fla.) argued on X earlier this month that the current Ethics process has a “massive problem,” saying “slow rolling investigations to protect party members is not due process. It is a cover up.”

The Democratic Women’s Caucus urged the panel to give an update on the status of their investigation into Gomez before the 60-day “blackout period” ahead of Election Day, which starts at the end of next week.

House Ethics Committee Chair Michael Guest (R-Miss.) told Bloomberg in April that the panel would be “receptive” to changes to speed up investigations.

▪ The Washington Post : The police investigation into how Miller’s daughter got hurt.

Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelensky looks on during his meeting with President Trump on the sidelines of the NATO summit in Ankara, Turkey, on July 8, 2026. (AP Photo/Alex Brandon)

NOT NOW : Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky rejected a call from his former defense chief for the country to hold new elections, saying that doing so during wartime would “split Ukraine apart.”

Former Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov called for an election last week in the aftermath of his firing from his role overseeing the country’s armed forces. Fedorov was popular and credited with helping modernize Ukraine’s forces with new technology and drone warfare, but Zelensky ousted him as Fedorov clashed with Ukraine’s top military commander.

Zelensky told reporters that holding elections now, still in the midst of war with Russia, would “pose enormous risks.”

“I believe elections during a war like this would generally pose enormous risks. Holding elections right now would be a tsunami for the state that would split Ukraine apart,” he said, according to The Associated Press .

Zelensky noted it was not the first such call but said no one has come up with a plan for holding elections safely, legitimately and democratically. Holding elections now would be complicated by the Ukrainian territory and citizens currently under Russian occupation, the Ukrainians who have fled abroad and those currently fighting on the front lines.

Trump and his allies have also previously called for Ukrainian elections, with the president even calling Zelensky a dictator. Ukraine noted the remarks seemed to echo a Russian disinformation campaign.

A presidential election was set to be held in 2024 but was postponed indefinitely amid the war. Zelensky said last year that he wouldn’t seek reelection to a second term after the war ends.

▪ CNN : Russia likely to mobilize 300,000 more troops, Zelensky says.

▪ The Guardian : Russia withdraws ambassador to U.K.

The right to worship shall not be infringed , Anti-Defamation League CEO and National Director Jonathan Greenblatt writes in The Hill.

Virginia may be building a national model for corrections , Jeff Bennett writes in The Hill.

Kyle Kirkwood poses for a photo after winning the IndyCar Freedom 250 Grand Prix auto race in Washington, on Aug. 23, 2026.

And finally … IndyCar driver Kyle Kirkwood won the Freedom 250 Grand Prix in Washington, D.C., on Sunday, capping off the summer of semiquincentennial events.

Kirkwood led the pack for most of the 147 laps, equal to 250 miles total, throughout the streets of the nation’s capital, passing by several key landmarks of the city. The cars reached speeds as high as 180 miles per hour during the race.

First lady Melania Trump took part in a relatively rare interview during the race, sharing how her father got her into racing as she was growing up.

“So, he introduced me to [the] design of the cars and the mechanics, and also the speed, and I loved it, every minute of it,” she said.

The president first called for the race in January, authorizing it with an executive order.

articles.title: Congress must now do its part on Medicare fraud
articles.summary: Vice President JD Vance urged Congress to codify recent healthcare fraud enforcement successes into permanent law to prevent future administrations from undoing the current administration’s progress.
articles.body:
When Vice President JD Vance — President Trump’s appointed fraud czar — stood before the Cabinet at Camp David at the end of July, he rattled off some eye-popping numbers. His team had uncovered $230 billion in fraud and stopped $56 billion of it before a dime went out the door.

A week later, Vance took the same case to Capitol Hill, hosting a roundtable with lawmakers and urging Congress to make the crackdown permanent rather than let it lapse with a future change in executive leadership.

Congress should heed his advice, and quickly. The relevant committees — Senate Finance and House Energy and Commerce chief among them — should draft legislation this fall that locks in the Medicare and Medicaid’s enforcement authority, funding levels, and enrollment moratoriums by statute.

Otherwise, everything this administration has built through executive and regulatory action can be undone the same way: by a future administration that simply chooses not to enforce the law. Only Congress can make these wins permanent.

The case for urgency is not abstract. Just this month, prosecutors in Philadelphia unsealed charges against 19 people in a home-healthcare scheme that reads almost like parody. One caregiver allegedly billed for visits made while she was traveling abroad. Another claimed to be caring for seven patients at once, racking up more billed hours than exist in a single day. The government says that one fraud ring alone cost taxpayers more than $4 million.

That is the kind of abuse the administration’s crackdown is built to catch. Under Health and Human Services Director Robert F. Kennedy Jr., CMS Administrator Mehmet Oz and Center for Medicare Director John Brooks, the executive branch has suspended billions of dollars in suspect Medicare payments, imposed nationwide moratoriums on new enrollment for hospice, home health , and durable medical equipment suppliers, and revoked billing privileges from thousands of providers.

This year’s national health care fraud takedown produced charges against more than 450 defendants tied to roughly $6 billion in alleged false claims. California and Minnesota have had more than $1 billion in Medicaid reimbursements frozen while they prove the money is reaching real patients.

But the same enforcement tools that catch fraud can just as easily overcorrect and choke off legitimate care — which is exactly why these decisions should not be left to agency discretion alone.

Take remote patient monitoring, the technology that lets seniors managing diabetes, high blood pressure, or heart disease take readings at home and send them straight to their care team, instead of waiting months for an appointment or driving hundreds of miles to a doctor’s office.

Regulators recently found real fraud in the program: companies cold-calling or robocalling seniors into monitoring plans they never asked for, then billing Medicare for monitoring that did not meaningfully happen. CMS deserves credit for catching it. But unelected career staff have now drafted a proposal broad enough to effectively kill physicians’ ability to use outside companies to run remote patient monitoring at all — even though those companies are often what keeps monitoring running for practices too short-staffed to do it themselves, in a country already facing a serious doctor shortage .

The problem with leaving fixes to rulemaking is that it makes overbroad fixes more likely. And either way, a future administrator can rewrite it again.

Congress doesn’t have that problem. Lawmakers could write a fix directly into statute — banning the cold-calling of beneficiaries that has fueled most of the abuse, and requiring a physician’s sign-off before any patient is enrolled. As the Heritage Foundation’s Peter St. Onge has noted , those two changes alone would stop most of the fraud without gutting a program that seniors, especially in underserved rural areas, depend on.

And that’s exactly what Congress should be across the board. It should take the enforcement gains the administration has already made, and the fixes still being worked out at the agency level, and write them into law before the moment passes.

Protecting Medicare from fraud should not be a partisan project. Both parties have an interest in a program that serves the seniors who paid into it for decades. The administration has done its part; the crackdown has been thorough and, so far, effective. As Vance made clear on Capitol Hill, the next move belongs to Congress. Lawmakers should introduce that bill while they still have the momentum to get it done.

Thomas Stratmann is a senior research fellow at the Mercatus Center and a professor of economics and law at George Mason University. He has a health economics research focus.

(AP Photo/Jacquelyn Martin)

articles.title: Is it finally time for a female president?
articles.summary: The next presidential election is more than two years away, but several women are already mentioned as possible candidates.
articles.body:
More than 200 women have sought the U.S. presidency in the last 250 years. Only Hillary Clinton in 2016 and Kamala Harris in 2024 became major-party nominees. No woman has ever won the nation’s most consequential job.

The next presidential election is more than two years away, but several women are already mentioned as possible candidates. Voters will be asked again to decide whether America is ready to elect its first female president. But that is the wrong question.

The correct question, of course, is which candidate has the right skills and qualities to lead America at this point in history. Voters shouldn’t select or reject a presidential candidate just because she’s a woman. Gender should not be a factor. The time will come when a woman finally breaks through the shatter-resistant ceiling that female candidates have encountered for so long. That ceiling is beginning to show some cracks, but it’s still fortified by stereotypes.

Politico reports that “Americans remain wary of electing a female president.” An American University poll “reveals a complicated portrait of how voters view women in politics.” Voters want to see more women in public office, but “bias and narrow expectations” surface when voters react to women in our highest office.

What expectations? “Empathy, inclusivity, and fresh perspectives are widely seen as unique strengths women bring to elected roles,” the poll found . However, while women are most trusted to address family-related issues, men are more trusted to deal with national security, foreign adversaries, crime and global conflicts.

“Women candidates also face a ‘double bind,'” states the poll’s write-up — they need to be “both ‘tough’ and ‘likable,’ a standard not typically applied to their male counterparts.”

Yet, tough and likable are not mutually exclusive qualities; empathy is not unique to women; and men care about family issues, too. Until voters shed these biases, they will deprive the country of some of its most talented and promising leaders.

At the same time, America would benefit from some of the qualities typically associated with women. The country is suffering from a hot mess of hypermasculinity. The president bullies and abuses allies. Pete Hegseth can’t get enough testosterone. Kash Patel acts like a frat bro. Stephen Miller has deported empathy from immigration policy. Whoever inherits the White House will have to dedicate enormous time, energy and political capital to repairing what’s left of government and reviving the rest of the world’s trust in America. That will require considerable “empathy, inclusivity, and fresh perspectives.”

Those are not inherently female qualities; they are human qualities traditionally coded as feminine. Voters need to make a significant attitude adjustment. They must understand the extraordinary value of the softer attributes, particularly as we try to heal the country and its relationships abroad. And they must broaden their understanding of toughness.

The 48th president will have to be a healer, a unifier, a firm but principled leader, sympathetic to the American people’s needs, reluctant to make war, and open to cooperation with the rest of the world. He or she must acknowledge that bullying and isolationism don’t work in a thoroughly interconnected world.

At this moment, we need a strong leader, but also a more mature understanding of what strength entails. It’s genuine rather than performative. It’s found in friendships, not isolation. It acknowledges, corrects and learns from mistakes, rather than distracting us from them. It serves the people rather than the person. At the same time, he or she must stand up to tyrants rather than becoming one of them. And while it remains true that America must defend peace with strength, strength means much more than military muscle. It requires domestic unity, the commitment to a common vision, and a commitment to one another.

I mentioned some early cracks in the shatter-proof ceiling. A study published in Political Behavior indicates that the process of redefining presidential strength may already be underway. “The traits that people associate with women politicians are more positive than 10 years ago and more congruent to desirable traits for politicians,” the researchers found.

Concurrently, respect for stereotypical male politicians and politics “shows a strong downfall compared to a decade ago.” The more positive view of women politicians and more negative view of their male counterparts corresponds with the Trump era.

Will there be a candidate who combines the best qualities of both? That’s what we should watch for as the next group of candidates emerges for the 2028 election.

William S. Becker is co-editor of and a contributor to “ Democracy Unchained: How to Rebuild Government for the People,” and a contributor to Democracy in a Hotter Time , named by the journal Nature as one of 2023’s five best science books. He previously served as a senior official in the Wisconsin Department of Justice. He is currently executive director of the Presidential Climate Action Project.

articles.title: Kyle Kirkwood wins Freedom 250 Grand Prix as IndyCar takes over DC
articles.summary: Kyle Kirkwood, an American IndyCar driver racing for Andretti Global, took home the checkered flag Sunday with a win at the Freedom 250 Grand Prix, the first professional motorsports road race ever run on the streets of Washington, D.C. The event, which was billed as a de facto finale to a slew of “America 250”…
articles.body:
Kyle Kirkwood, an American IndyCar driver racing for Andretti Global, took home the checkered flag Sunday with a win at the Freedom 250 Grand Prix , the first professional motorsports road race ever run on the streets of Washington, D.C.

The event, which was billed as a de facto finale to a slew of “America 250” celebrations in the District this summer, was heavy on symbols of American pride and attended by President Trump and other top Cabinet officials.

Sunday’s race day drew tens of thousands to the nation’s capital and shuttered much of the National Mall and downtown D.C. in the days leading up to the event.

With his win, Kirkwood notched his seventh career IndyCar victory and his sixth on a street course, raking in key IndyCar series points with just two weeks remaining in the racing league’s season.

A Jupiter, Fla., native and one of eight Americans in the field, Kirkwood made a point of referencing Trump directly during a postrace interview after speeding away with a lead that lasted more than 125 laps on Sunday.

“I’m almost in tears here. This is a big moment for us and a big moment for America with the 250,” Kirkwood said.

“I’m a fellow Florida guy, I live up in Jupiter,” he said, pointing to the area where the president was watching. “It’s cool to see him down here. And what a place to do it. If you can’t win the Indy 500, this is definitely the place to win.”

Trump began Sunday’s race by waving the green flag after his motorcade drove a ceremonial first lap around the 1.7-mile track featuring seven turns and weaving through some of D.C.’s most iconic monuments and federal buildings.

Secretary of the Interior Doug Burgum was seen on television coverage atop the pre-race podium and screamed into a microphone when it was time for drivers to “start your engines.”

Burgum is one of several top Trump officials who had been tasked with selling the event as a moment of unity for the country, even as local critics raised noise and vibration concerns.

“This is the perfect time to do this. Congress is on recess, the economic development of D.C., the people here all love this idea,” Burgum argued during an interview on Fox News just hours before the race.

“I’m a DC resident. Please DON’T do this again next year,” wrote the left-leaning influencer and media personality Aaron Parnas on the social platform X, responding to a clip of Burgum’s remark.

The president was seen visiting with top government leaders, business officials and executives at IndyCar during the nearly three-hour-long race, while Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy was tasked with waving the checkered flag as Kirkwood soared through the finish line.

Kirkwood finished four seconds ahead of Denmark native Christian Lundgaard, averaging 93.2 mph and gaining an additional 40 IndyCar Series points on leader Álex Palou, one of the icons of the sport who struggled in D.C. on Sunday, finishing 20th out of 25.

Throughout the weekend, the roars of the IndyCar and bustling pit crews could be heard for blocks across downtown, as some residents complained about traffic, long lines to get into the racetrack and noisy flyovers as part of the celebration.

Elected Democrats, meanwhile, suggested Sunday’s first-of-its-kind event sent an out-of-touch message to Americans across the country.

“While you struggle with the cost of gas, Trump offers you the spectacle of an IndyCar race hoping you will not notice,” Sen. Adam Schiff (D-Calif.) wrote in one social media post on Sunday. “More taxpayer money spent on his self-aggrandizing distractions. And you get higher taxes and higher costs.”

College football begins this weekend, thrusting a debate about the future of what it means to be a student-athlete into the spotlight once again. Some observers expressed outrage online over reports that star University of South Carolina quarterback LaNorris Sellers is not taking any classes this fall before he graduates this December. Sen. Bill Cassidy (R-La.), who has yet to signal support for the Protect College Sports Act, responded in a social media post that he had proposed an amendment requiring athletes to be enrolled and making progress toward a degree. “We are seeing too many cases where the ‘student’ in student-athlete is becoming optional,” the Republican said.

Sen. Eric Schmitt (R-Mo.) appears to be enjoying his recess. The Republican spent the weekend in St. Louis, where the PGA Tour’s BMW Championship was being held. Schmitt played in the tournament’s pro-am alongside world No. 1 player Scottie Scheffler, who is fresh off a win in Memphis and is looking to make a run for another FedEx Cup title.

An Alabama jury on Thursday awarded $9.25 million in damages after finding that The New York Times defamed Kai Spears, a college basketball player at the University of Alabama, by incorrectly reporting that he was at the scene of a fatal shooting in Tuscaloosa. Three other basketball players from the school were present at the January 2023 shooting, and Spears’s attorney praised the judge’s ruling. The Times could still appeal the decision.

Jocks on the Hill: Sen. Chris Coons (D-Del.)

Sen. Chris Coons, one of several Democrats working with Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) to get the Protect College Sports Act passed once lawmakers return from recess, answered some sports questions for The Hill.

“Football. I played in high school, my son-in-law and father-in-law played. I married into a Penn State-obsessed family. My father-in-law and brother-in-law made me take a quiz about Penn State football before I married my wife, and I flunked it cold. If it wasn’t for my now mother-in-law, I don’t think I would have made it. It’s something that’s bonded our family.”

“Our other son Jack went to Notre Dame, and we’ve become a big Notre Dame family. So in the fall, I’m watching Eagles, Notre Dame, Penn State pretty much every weekend, and my wife Annie is a huge football fan.”

Is there an athlete you looked up to growing up?

“The Flyers, Sixers and Phillies in the late ’70s, early ’80s. … I was pretty focused on high school sports, though. The Phillies won the World Series when I was a junior in high school, and Dallas Green’s son was a classmate of mine, so we followed him pretty closely.”

Hate is a strong word, but is there a team you love to root against?

“Ohio State, for sure. Sometimes Michigan. The Commanders, I almost said the Redskins, and you know … Dallas, Dallas, Dallas.”

Sports and politics are both full of cliches, what’s one that resonates with you?

It’s no secret the NFL has international ambition, but The Athletic’s Jayna Bardahl writes on what the feasibility of an overseas NFL team would be and what challenges such a club would face.

For those of you closely following the Los Angeles Lakers-Buss family succession drama, The Ringer’s Katie Baker has a great story here laying out how “sibling squabbles, legal battles — and now a contested sale could end the family’s claim on the franchise once and for all.”

It’s never too early to start speculating which performer might get the Super Bowl gig next February, right? Sports Illustrated notes prediction markets are currently favoring hip-hop icon Jay-Z over Justin Bieber and Miley Cyrus.
